rv.q: Onstage, imagination can indeed turn a scrap-metal capsule into a soaring rocket, and send Matha, suspended by wires, spinning through space.
It all looks sumptuous, and the play’s vibrant, optimistic world is a pleasant one to get lost in, even if – like the unsuccessful mission it depicts – it never quite reaches a satisfying conclusion.
The Afronauts confirms his promise, and exudes a winning warmth.
An entertaining play, but it feels like Cameron lacked the patience to write a great one.
The rest is a fascinating story told in familiar strokes.
It’s an interesting story that heads in many directions but ends up lost and atmosphere-less.
Instead, we’re put through the most tedious evening at the Royal Court in London since the days under the previous management when the venue was turning out one dud after another.
The Afronauts is a funny, bruising and beautifully realised play that earns its running time and then some.
It proves accessible, in places enlightening, and a surprisingly entertaining vehicle despite the deployment of a little historical licence and a slightly overlong first half.
Cameron’s ambitious play certainly reaches for the stars, but unfortunately it doesn’t quite get there, even as designer Gilmour’s wonderfully homemade spaceship heads for the skies.
The Afronauts does not represent a crash landing for one of Britain’s brightest talents, but the alchemy hasn’t quite worked this time round.
Instead, it bewilders and disappoints—despite a strong cast and substantial budget, this production does not have the right stuff.

Bolstered by exceptional performances, spectacular design and an utterly magnificent score, The Afronauts recaptures that increasingly rare, almost childlike sense of wonder that theatre is uniquely equipped to offer.
A visually stunning, beautifully performed and wonderfully optimistic piece of theatre that reminds us just how extraordinary the human imagination can be.
The Afronauts is an uplifting, joyful and wonderfully playful celebration of ambition, imagination and the audacity to dream beyond the limits others set for you.
Ryan Calais Cameron’s play has a witty script full of brilliant one-liners, managing to be funny while also taking its subject matter seriously.
Our problem with it is that it needs a good edit currently and to lose at least half an hour before the doubtless fascinating story at its heart can be emphasised with the clarity it deserves.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Ryan Calais Cameron's ambitious Zambian space race drama: some find it joyful and visually stunning, others say its big ideas never fully lift off. Lucian Msamati's performance earns consistent praise.
